## How do we know our function is correct? {data-timing="30"}

### Testing Python functions

**Computing Bootcamp | Thursday 8 October 2026**

Today: predict behaviour, check it, explain what the check detects, and rerun.

::: notes
00:00-00:30. This is a ten-minute opening before the testing walkthrough.
Students can watch without typing. State that code running without an error does
not mean that it produced the right result.
:::

## What does testing mean? {data-timing="180"}

**A test is an explicit, repeatable check of an expected behaviour.**

```python
assert count_above([8, 12, 10, 15], 10) == 2
```

| Part | Question |
|:--|:--|
| Input | What do we give the function? |
| Expected result | What do the stated rules predict? |
| Observed result | What does the function actually return? |

- The test passes when the observed and expected results agree.
- A passing test is **evidence**, not proof that the program is always correct.

::: notes
00:30-03:30. Ask for the expected count before showing or running the assertion.
The values 12 and 15 exceed 10; the value 10 does not. Explain that a useful
test begins with an independently justified expectation. Passing assertions are
silent; a false condition raises AssertionError. Do not introduce doctest or
pytest syntax here.
:::

## Why do we test? {data-timing="180"}

- Code can run successfully and still produce the wrong scientific result.
- Tests make assumptions and ambiguous rules visible.
- Boundary cases expose faults that ordinary examples can miss.
- Repeatable checks help other people verify and reproduce our work.
- Rerunning tests shows whether a later change broke existing behaviour.

> Several passing tests increase our confidence; they do not test every possible input.

::: notes
03:30-06:30. Connect testing to scientific reasoning: an error message is not
required for a result to be wrong. A test records a claim about behaviour in a
form that can be rerun. Emphasise that the choice of cases matters as much as
the number of tests.
:::

## Use more than one kind of case {.smaller data-timing="150"}

| Case | Question | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Normal** | Does typical valid input work? | Heights above and below 10 |
| **Boundary** | What happens at an edge? | A height exactly equal to 10 |
| **Failure** | Is invalid input handled clearly? | A count that is not numeric |

```python
assert count_above([8, 12, 10, 15], 10) == 2  # normal
assert count_above([10], 10) == 0             # boundary
assert count_above([], 10) == 0               # boundary
```

**What could still be wrong if only the normal test passes?**

::: notes
06:30-09:00. Ask students to predict each result. Use the exact-threshold case
to expose a possible greater-than versus greater-than-or-equal mistake. The
empty-list case checks the stopping and initial-value behaviour. The table's
invalid count is a failure-case example for the observations exercise; do not
imply that count_above must perform that conversion.
:::

## Today: predict → test → explain → rerun {data-timing="60"}

1. Complete your own function attempt and checks.
2. Predict what the prepared faulty function will return.
3. Write a boundary test that exposes its incorrect assumption.
4. Explain why the ordinary tests did not detect the fault.
5. Rerun your own checks in a fresh Python process.

[Open the independent observations exercise](https://mulquabio.github.io/MQB/notebooks/python.html#independent-exercise-summarise-observations-by-site)

[Open the faulty-function critique](https://mulquabio.github.io/MQB/notebooks/python.html#can-your-tests-detect-a-plausible-wrong-answer)

::: notes
09:00-10:00. Hand over to the chapter. Students first work individually, then
compare predictions and tests in their assigned pairs. Every student retains
and reruns their own implementation and tests. The prepared function is a
deliberately faulty teaching example, not a reference solution.
:::
